'''Steven Soter''' is an astrophysicist currently holding the positions of scientist-in-residence for [[New York University]]'s Environmental Studies Program and of Research Associate for the Department of Astrophysics at the [[American Museum of Natural History]]. He is a proponent of the [[International Astronomical Union]]'s [[IAU definition of planet|definition of planet]].

==Education==
Soter received his [[bachelor's degree]] in astronomy and physics from [[UCLA]] in 1965 (advisors [[George O. Abell|George Abell]] and [[Peter Goldreich]]) and his doctorate in astronomy from [[Cornell University]] in 1971 (advisors [[Thomas Gold]], [[Carl Sagan]], and [[Joseph A. Burns|Joseph Burns]]).

==Career in astrophysics==
In 1974, Soter suggested that dust produced by meteoritic bombardment of Saturn's moon [[Phoebe (moon)|Phoebe]] might orbit the planet until colliding with Saturn's moon [[Iapetus (moon)|Iapetus]] and be responsible for the unique dark-bright dichotomy of the latter. Although not the unique cause, dust originating from [[Saturn]]'s [[irregular moon|irregular satellites]] was later found in data from the [[Cassini-Huygens|Cassini spacecraft]] to indeed play a crucial role in the coloration of [[Iapetus (moon)|Iapetus]].<ref name="Denk">{{Cite journal
| last1 = Denk | first1 = Tilmann 
| title = Iapetus: Unique Surface Properties and a Global Color Dichotomy from Cassini Imaging

| date = 2010-01-22

| journal = [[Science (journal)|Science]] | volume =  327| issue =5964 | pages =432–435
| date = 2010-01-22 | doi = 10.1126/science.1177132 | pmid = 20007862|bibcode = 2010Sci...327..432S | s2cid = 20663944 }}</ref> The discovery of Saturn's "[[Rings of Saturn#Phoebe ring|Phoebe ring]]" in 2009 further strengthened the probability that this process first described by Soter plays a significant role in shaping [[Iapetus (moon)|Iapetus]]'s appearance.<ref name = "Verbiscer">{{cite journal|last=Verbiscer|first=Anne|author2=Skrutskie, Michael |author3=Hamilton, Douglas  |title=Saturn's largest ring|journal=[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]|doi=10.1038/nature08515|date=2009-10-07|pmid=19812546|volume=461|issue=7267|pages=1098–100|bibcode = 2009Natur.461.1098V |s2cid=4349726 }}</ref><ref name=sciencenews_large_ring>{{cite journal|last=Cowen|first=Rob|url=http://www.sciencenews.org/view/generic/id/48097/title/Largest_known_planetary_ring_discovered|title=Largest known planetary ring discovered|journal=[[Science News]]|date=2009-10-06}}</ref>

In 1977-1979, Soter co-wrote, along with Carl Sagan and [[Ann Druyan]], Carl Sagan's monumental 1980 astronomy documentary series ''[[Cosmos: A Personal Voyage|Cosmos]]''. Since then, he has also acted as advisor on a number of science documentaries, such as the IMAX films ''[[Blue Planet (1990 film)|Blue Planet]]'' and ''[[Cosmic Voyage (1996 film)|Cosmic Voyage]]''.

In 1997, Soter took a position at the [[American Museum of Natural History]]'s [[Hayden Planetarium]], and eventually progressed to the position of research associate. He also made significant contributions to research related to the ancient Greek city [[Helike]].

In 2007, after the IAU voted on a [[IAU definition of planet|definition of planet]], Soter published an article<ref name="Soter2007"/> in ''[[Scientific American]]'' in which he outlined a mathematical formulation, the "planetary discriminant," to describe how the IAU's requirement that a planet must have "[[Clearing the neighbourhood|cleared its neighborhood]]" of other objects might be applied in practice. He had already written a more technical article on the same subject in 2006, submitted to ''The Astronomical Journal'' before the IAU resolution.<ref name="Soter2006"/>

In 2014, he partnered with Druyan again to co-write a new television miniseries, ''[[Cosmos: A Spacetime Odyssey]]'', hosted by his AMNH colleague [[Neil deGrasse Tyson]].
